passage:
Honestly, what stopped me was a guideline I almost skipped, so I'm glad I read it. I'm Noor, and last spring I was told to summarise a forty-page client contract. The quickest way was to paste it into a chatbot on the internet. My hand was already on the mouse.

But something nagged me, so I opened the company's AI guideline first. It said clearly that client documents must never go into public services, and that only approved tools were allowed. I then asked my manager Gargi which tool I could use. She smiled and pointed me to the internal one. It was slower, and I read a lot more myself. But the client's name never left our systems, and I slept fine.

qa.q: How many pages was the client contract?
What was Noor feeling when something nagged before pasting the contract?
qa.a: Noor felt uneasy and cautious, sensing a possible mistake even with a hand already on the mouse.

qa.q: What could Noor do if the internal tool could not handle the contract, and why?
qa.a: Noor could tell Gargi and ask for another approved way to get help, because the rule protects the client and a workaround would break it.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Noor's question about approved tools?
qa.a: Gargi likely felt pleased, seeing a team member who checks the rules first and can be trusted with client material.

grounding: The employee checks the company AI guideline before pasting client documents into a public chatbot and asks the manager about approved tools.

I'm Saurabh, and I've shared a desk row with Omkar since he joined the consulting team in May. On his third Monday, a client sent a forty-page contract and our lead wanted a summary by noon.
I saw Omkar open a public chatbot in one tab and the contract in another. His cursor hovered over the paste box. Then he stopped, closed the chatbot, and searched the company intranet instead. He read the one-page guideline twice, scrolling back to a line in bold.
He walked to our manager's cabin and I heard him ask, "Can we put client documents into public tools, or is there an approved one?" The manager pointed him to the firm's internal tool.
The summary reached the lead at twelve fifteen, a little late. I don't know if Omkar was nervous or just careful, but nobody had to report anything.

qa.q: What did Omkar search after closing the chatbot?
qa.a: He searched the company intranet and read the one-page guideline twice.

qa.q: What might Omkar have been feeling as his cursor hovered over the paste box?
qa.a: He may have felt uneasy and unsure, torn between the noon deadline and the risk of putting a client contract into a public tool.

qa.q: Which approach would suit a rushed deadline like this, and why?
qa.a: Asking early about approved tools, even before a deadline arrives, would let the summary be done on time without risking confidential data.

qa.q: How does Omkar's choice look to Saurabh at the next desk?
qa.a: Saurabh sees careful, slightly slow work and cannot tell if Omkar was nervous, but notices that nothing had to be reported.

grounding: Shows an employee checking the company guideline before pasting client documents into a public chatbot and asking the manager about approved tools.

passage:
Day one. Vijay, three weeks into his first analyst job at an accounting firm, had a client's payroll spreadsheet open and a public chatbot in the next tab. It would take seconds. He paused, thinking of the client's staff names and bank details in those rows, and searched the intranet for "AI" instead. A policy existed. He bookmarked it and went home.
Day two. He read it on the metro: no client data in any tool the firm hasn't approved. At work he asked his manager, Anirban, "Which tools can I use for client files?" Anirban showed him the internal assistant and added him to the access list that afternoon.
Day nine. A teammate leaned over. "Just paste it into the free one, it's faster." Vijay shook his head and opened the internal assistant. "Policy says no. This one's allowed."

qa.q: Where did Vijay read the policy on day two?
qa.a: He read it on the metro.

qa.q: Why did Vijay pause before pasting the spreadsheet, and how did he feel?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, thinking of the client's staff names and bank details in the rows, so he stopped and looked for a policy first.

qa.q: What else could Vijay do to help the rest of the team?
qa.a: He could share the policy link and the name of the approved tool in the team chat, so others do not have to guess.

qa.q: How might the teammate see Vijay's refusal on day nine?
qa.a: The teammate may find Vijay a little rigid at first, but hearing a clear 'policy says no' with an allowed option might make them rethink the shortcut too.

grounding: Shows an employee reading the firm's AI guideline before pasting client documents into a public tool and asking the manager which tools are approved.
